newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault plant closure may cut jobs, not output.
newsitem.headline: Renault plant closure may cut jobs, not output.

text.p: French carmaker Renault is the second company this year to announce cutbacks in its European car operations after running up huge losses in a market plagued by excess production capacity.

But industry analysts are uncertain whether the move is merely a bid by Renault to cut costs by shedding jobs or represents a wider trend to reduce the overcapacity that has made it very hard for car companies to turn a profit in Europe.

Renault, the weakling of Europe's "Big Six" carmakers, said on Thursday that it would close Renault Industrie Belgique (RIB) which employs 3,100 people as part of an effort to streamline its manufacturing operations.
Its announcement came a month after Ford Motor Co said it would cut 1,300 jobs at its Halewood plant in Britain. Ford reduced the number to 980 in early February after unions threatened to strike.
"What you're seeing is that the manufacturers making losses in Europe, Ford and Renault, are having to deal with those losses and take out cost," said analyst Nick Snee at JP Morgan.
In a statement announcing the closure of its Belgian plant, Renault said the move was imperative because its 1996 results would be "negative and quite significantly so".

After a previous profit warning from Renault earlier this month, analysts pencilled in estimates for a 1996 loss of around two billion francs for Renault before restructuring provisions. They also expect the company to lose money this year.
Its domestic rival, PSA Peugeot Citroen , is expected to show a profit for 1996, but analysts estimate it will be down 30 percent after having fallen 45 percent in 1995.

Renault announced the plant closure a day after the French government turned down a joint request by the two carmakers to finance the bulk of 40,000 early retirements, representing 15 percent of their combined work forces, over six years.
Defending the decision, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Friday the scheme would have cost several billion francs and the government did not have the means to pay for it.

"The state is the taxpayer and the state's role is not to come constantly to the rescue of companies who need to remedy their difficulties," he told French radio, adding that both firms would have to restructure to face increasing competition.

Renault, and to a lesser extent the PSA group, ran into trouble last year because although European car sales rose 6.5 percent in 1996, profit margins were eroded by a fierce price war among carmakers producing far in excess of demand.

"I estimate there's capacity in Europe to produce 16 to 16.5 million cars, and last year 13 million were sold," said analyst John Lawson at Salomon Brothers. Some experts calculate capacity in Europe is as much as 18 million units.
"By historic standards, (sales) volumes in Europe are OK," Keith Hayes at Goldman Sachs said.
"They could even grow 10 percent in the next three to four years, but that's not enough to deal with the chronic excess capacity in Europe that's the cause of these problems."
Renault Industrie Belgique employs 3,100 people assembling Megane and Clio models, but Renault said the output could be matched by the equivalent of 1,900 jobs at other plants.
Unions called the move "unbelievably brutal", but investors drove up Renault's stock nearly five percent late on Thursday on relief that it was starting to address some of its problems.

Analysts say cost-cutting alone cannot solve the difficulties facing the French carmakers, whose economies of scale are low compared with European leader Volkswagen , which produces twice as many vehicles as either French firm.
They are also too dependent on the European market, generating less than 15 percent of sales outside western Europe.
"Look at Fiat ," one analyst said. "It's not making money in Europe. Its figures were boosted by its Brazilian and Polish operations."
Competition in Europe will only get fiercer with the market set to open up fully to Asian imports in the year 2000.
"It's a mystery why France feels the need to have two carmakers," another analyst said.
